find: Tear resistance is highest parallel to the grain direction.
replace: Tear resistance is lowest along the grain — paper tears easily and in a straight line in the grain direction, and needs more force to tear across it.
note: F1: tear resistance direction reversed; paper tears most easily along the grain, so resistance is highest across it. Contradicted the lesson's own flashcard and glossary.

find: paper is considerably stiffer when bent against the grain
replace: paper is stiffer along the grain, the direction in which the fibres lie
note: F2: contradicted the Key Fact and the knowledge-check answer key, which both say paper is stiffer along the grain.

find: a thick, slightly textured paper (90–135 g/m²)
replace: a thick, slightly textured paper (120–150 g/m²)
note: F3: cartridge paper is normally taught as 120-150 gsm; 90 gsm is layout/copier territory.

expect:
Students may include:
- During manufacture, paper fibres align in the machine direction (grain direction).
- Paper and board are considerably stiffer when bent against the grain, so aligning the grain along the fold lines reduces the force needed to score and crease.
- Folding against the grain can crack the surface coating and weaken the structure of the carton.
- Specifying grain direction correctly during print finishing reduces waste and improves the quality of the assembled box. [4 marks: 1 mark per clear, developed point]
value:
Students may include:
- During manufacture, paper fibres align in the machine direction (grain direction).
- Paper and board are harder to fold across the grain, so aligning the grain along the fold lines reduces the force needed to score and crease.
- Folding against the grain can crack the surface coating and weaken the structure of the carton.
- Specifying grain direction correctly during print finishing reduces waste and improves the quality of the assembled box. [4 marks: 1 mark per clear, developed point]
note: F4: mark scheme repeated the reversed grain-stiffness claim from F2.

find: a simple rule of thumb is that 1 micron ≈ 1 g/m² for uncoated boards
replace: a simple rule of thumb is that an uncoated board is about 1.4 microns thick for every 1 g/m² of weight
note: F5: the 1:1 rule contradicted the lesson's own figures (280-350 gsm board quoted as 400-500 microns, i.e. about 1.4 microns per gsm).

find: moderate cost. Used for food packaging, cereal boxes and cosmetics cartons where a high-quality printed surface is required at moderate cost.
note: F6: the duplex bullet repeated the same sentence twice.

find: This is the international standard used across all Eduqas specification and design work.
replace: This is the international standard used across design, print and packaging work.
note: F7: house rule - the exam board must never be named in student-facing prose.

find: bonding two or more plies of material together increases bending stiffness far more than adding the same total thickness as a single ply
replace: bonding two or more plies of material together builds up thickness, and bending stiffness rises with roughly the cube of thickness, so doubling the thickness makes a board about eight times stiffer
note: F8: a bonded laminate is not stiffer than a solid sheet of the same total thickness; the real gain comes from the extra thickness.

expect: Bonding layers together increases bending stiffness far more than a single ply of equal total thickness.
value: It builds up thickness, and bending stiffness rises with roughly the cube of thickness, so a thicker laminate is far stiffer.
note: F8: flashcard repeated the same wrong comparison.

find: uncoated cartridge (80–120 g/m²) for books and letterheads
replace: uncoated bond or offset paper (80–120 g/m²) for books and letterheads
note: F9: cartridge is a drawing paper, not a book or letterhead stock, and 80 gsm is well below its normal 120-150 gsm band.

expect: What is imposition in print finishing?
note: F10: the spec lists imposition under pre-press operations, not finishing.
F11: 'liner' is the correct trade term for label backing paper, so the key marked a right answer wrong.

find: plastic carrier bags, food wrappers and newspaper supplements
replace: plastic carrier bags, food wrappers and self-adhesive labels
note: F12: newspapers and their supplements are printed by web offset or gravure, not flexography.

find: when sent to landfill or composted, they break down naturally within months rather than centuries, unlike plastics
replace: in compost or soil they break down within months rather than the centuries plastics take, although waste buried in landfill breaks down far more slowly
note: F13: buried landfill waste has little oxygen, so paper does not break down in months there.

expect: It breaks down naturally within months in landfill or composting, not over hundreds of years.
value: In compost or soil it breaks down within months, not the hundreds of years plastics take.
note: F13: flashcard repeated the landfill claim.

expect:
Advantages of paper and board:
- Paper and board are biodegradable and break down naturally within months in landfill or composting conditions, unlike rigid plastics which persist for hundreds of years.
- Paper fibre is recyclable up to five to seven times and is collected and processed through a well-established, near-universal UK kerbside recycling infrastructure, giving high actual recycling rates (above 70% for packaging board).
- Paper and board are made from a renewable resource (managed forestry) certified by bodies such as the FSC, unlike petroleum-based plastics which depend on a finite fossil fuel supply.
- Consumer perception of paper-based packaging is strongly positive; research consistently shows that shoppers associate cardboard packaging with environmental responsibility, which supports brand values in environmentally aware markets.
Disadvantages of paper and board:
- Paper and board provide little barrier to moisture and oxygen without additional coatings or laminates, limiting their use in packaging wet, fatty or oxygen-sensitive products compared with plastics that provide an inherent barrier.
- Rigid plastic packaging is generally lighter per unit volume than board, reducing transport emissions per product; it also offers superior impact protection for fragile goods.
- Multi-material paper and board constructions (foil-lined cartons, laminated board) are difficult to recycle and in practice are often sent to landfill or energy recovery, undermining the recyclability advantage.
- Paper and board packaging typically has a shorter functional life before it loses structural integrity under moisture or handling, whereas rigid plastic containers can be reused many times.
[8 marks - Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion across sustainability, functional performance and consumer perception with at least two developed points on each side. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages identified with some development across at least two of the three dimensions. Developing: Points listed with limited development; coverage of only one dimension. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial response.]
